nameStory: The carrot seed moth gets its common name from its larvae's love affair with wild carrot plants, particularly their developing seeds. These little moths are practically synonymous with the feathery white blooms of Queen Anne's lace (wild carrot), where they spend their youth munching on the very seeds that will become next year's carrot patch.
description: The carrot seed moth is a small, delicate member of the snout moth family that arrived in New England relatively recently - the first one was spotted in North America in 2002! These petite moths have wingspans roughly the size of a quarter to a half-dollar, measuring about an inch to an inch and a third across. They're most active during the warm summer months of June and July, when you might spot them fluttering around wild carrot and other plants in the parsley family.

idTips.label: Wingspan
idTips.description: Small moth with wings spanning roughly 1 to 1.3 inches across - about the size of a quarter to a half-dollar coin when fully spread

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a somewhat erratic, bouncing pattern typical of snout moths, often staying close to carrot family plants

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender body typical of crambid moths, with a subtle snout-like projection of the mouthparts when viewed up close

idTips.label: Activity Time
idTips.description: Most active during twilight hours and at night, occasionally seen during daytime resting on or near host plants

idTips.label: Host Plant Association
idTips.description: Nearly always found near wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace), fennel, or other plants in the parsley family where they lay eggs

habitat: Look for carrot seed moths in sunny, open areas where wild carrots and other plants in the parsley family thrive - think old fields, meadows, roadsides, and garden edges. They're particularly fond of disturbed soils and waste areas where Queen Anne's lace commonly grows. You'll also find them around herb gardens where fennel and other umbelliferous plants are cultivated.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; larvae may still be developing in overwintering sites or pupating in preparation for summer emergence.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through July when adults emerge to mate and lay eggs. This is the best time to spot them flying around carrot family plants during evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as the new generation of larvae feeds on developing seeds of host plants. Moths become increasingly scarce as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; the species overwinters in larval or pupal stage, hidden away until the following summer's warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: This European moth is such a recent immigrant to North America that many field guides don't even include it yet - you could be spotting a species that your grandparents never had the chance to see in New England!
confusionNotes: Since this is the only Sitochroa species in New England, confusion mainly occurs with other small crambid moths in the same size range. The key difference is the carrot seed moth's strong association with wild carrot and related plants - if you see small moths consistently hanging around Queen Anne's lace, you're likely looking at carrot seed moths.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'carrot seed' moth, this species actually prefers wild carrots (Queen Anne's lace) over garden carrots, though both plants are the same species. The moth's recent arrival in North America makes it an interesting example of how species continue to expand their ranges in our interconnected world.
compareHints: As the only Sitochroa species in New England, the carrot seed moth is most easily compared to other small crambid snout moths in the region. Unlike many of its relatives that feed on grasses or other plant families, this species is distinctly tied to the parsley family plants. Its consistent association with wild carrot and fennel, combined with its summer flight period, helps distinguish it from other small moths in the crambid family that might have different host plants or flight times.
